extracted.intended_audience: writers, actors, opera practitioners, and critics interested in theatrical technique, comic writing, and characterization
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical observations about theatrical acting, opera staging, chorus practice, pantomime/political satire, and comic/literary characterisation aimed at improving performance and humorous writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting should be done 'off' rather than naturalistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting, as I understand by the term, it is done 'off.' This is not my idea of acting. But I do not see how you are going to substitute for it anything more natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances should be theatrical rather than literal reproductions of real behaviour: examples include not trying to act exactly how a wounded man would behave while singing, or attempting realistic resistance when you must sing. Anti-patterns: trying to 'act naturally' in situations that would prevent singing or clear stage business (e.g., pushing against a door while delivering a long aria).

rubrics_metrics.name: In opera, everything must be sacrificed to musical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: In opera, everything is rightly sacrificed to musical necessity. The experienced artist takes the centre of the stage and husbands his resources. ... he leaves it to the composer to make clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging and acting choices should prioritize musical structure and requirements; performers should conserve physical and vocal resources, accept theatrical conventions that aid musical clarity, and avoid naturalistic interruptions of musical flow. Composer's musical intent supersedes realistic stage-behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage business must support the music and singing (avoid realistic behaviour that conflicts with performance needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are singing at the top of your voice, you don’t want a heavy woman hanging round your neck. ... If a mob is climbing the stairs thirsting for your blood, you do not want to stand upright with your arms stretched out ... while you go over at some length the varied incidents leading up to the annoyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical staging: do not stage realistic physical reactions that would compromise vocal delivery or musical pacing. Instead use stylised, concise stage actions that allow singing to proceed; plan choreography so performers can portray the situation without undermining the music or intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: The operatic chorus should be experienced, unified, and visually coordinated
rubrics_metrics.description: The great thing required of that operatic chorus is experience. The young and giddy-pated the chorus master has no use for. The sober, honest, industrious lady or gentleman, with a knowledge of music is very properly his ideal. What I admire about the chorus chiefly is its unity. The whole village dresses exactly alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select chorus members for sobriety, discipline and musical competence rather than novelty or youth. Ensure unity in movement, costume and grouping (pre-arranged meetings, matched partners/heights, organized children's groups) so the chorus reads as a single pictorial element onstage; anti-patterns include rivalry in dress or undisciplined individualism that breaks the ensemble effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic spectacle should not be expected to replace other arts; the composer should aim to make listeners forget other artistic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be done, Herr Wagner, believe me. You cannot substitute the music drama for all the arts combined. The object to be aimed at by the wise composer should be to make us, while listening to his music, forgetful of all remaining artistic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While visual spectacle can enhance opera, it should not be used as a wholesale substitute for painting, statuary, or other arts; the primary task is musical and dramatic cohesion so the audience is absorbed in the music rather than treating the stage as a rolling picture gallery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect operatic chorus to substitute for high-class statuary; manage audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the most daring hope of all was the dream that came to Herr Wagner that his opera singers, his grouped choruses, would eventually satisfy the craving of the public for high class statuary. ... I should doubt the average operatic chorus being regarded by the connoisseur as a cheap and pleasant substitute for a bas relief from the Elgin marbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers/composers should not market choruses as replacements for fine visual arts; the chorus's strength lies in musical unity and experience, not in becoming a static object of sculptural admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: When including topical politics in pantomime, aim for innocent raillery that offends neither side
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper attitude to have assumed towards it was that of innocent raillery, free from all trace of partisanship. ... 'a bright, amusing resumé of the whole problem that should give offence to neither side.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a pantomime or comic review addresses a hot political question, present a light-hearted, non-partisan summary suitable for broad audiences. The piece should be up-to-date and witty without advocating a political stance; practical advice: craft a bright, amusing resumé rather than polemic, to keep the entertainment accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic writing can and should find the amusing side of disasters and public events
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything has its amusing side, I told myself. One turns out comic stories about funerals, about weddings. Hardly a misfortune that can happen to mankind but has produced its comic literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humorists may treat tragedies and misfortunes as material, provided they find an angle that reveals irony or absurdity. Use restraint and craft to transform grim material into comic perspective rather than gratuitous mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make characters (especially heroines) human by allowing them passions and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroine with passions, instincts, emotions, is to be welcomed. But I want her to grasp the fact that after all she is only one of us. I should like her better if, instead of demanding: 'What is wrong in civilisation?' ... she would occasionally say to herself: 'Guess I've made a fool of myself this time. I do feel that 'shamed of myself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating sympathetic protagonists, prefer complex, fallible characters who acknowledge their mistakes. Avoid conventionally 'angelic' heroines who never err; giving a character self-awareness and acceptance of blame increases reader respect and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction should consider plausible, ordinary alternatives rather than contrived impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Why could not Faust have married the girl? ... There was nothing in the bond to the effect that Faust should not marry, so far as we are told. ... If Faust said to himself: 'I should like to marry the girl, but I won't do it; it would not be fair to the Old Man'—if this was the way Faust looked at the matter there is nothing more to be said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should examine whether simpler, realistic solutions (e.g., marriage, ordinary domestic life) would have been available to characters before resorting to melodramatic or implausible plot devices. If an extraordinary constraint is asserted (e.g., a bond with the devil), it should be made explicit and credible within the narrative; otherwise readers will question character motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complacent racial or civilisational caricatures; account for change and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose fresh sap be stirring through his three hundred millions? We thought he was so very dead; we thought the time had come to cut him up and divide him ... If the Chinaman be not dead? If the cutting-up process has only served to waken him?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and satirists should be wary of fixed, dismissive stereotypes about whole peoples or cultures; consider historical dynamism and the possibility of political, social or cultural revival. Using caricature risks missing important future changes and can produce foolish complacency in satire.
